items.title: Access policy defines element-level rights, granting and revocation
items.statement: An access policy, registered by the economic operator once per product type and named when a passport is created or updated, assigns every data element of the passport exactly one of the access classes public, legitimateInterest and authority; header attributes are always public, and an element no rule reaches falls to the policy's default or, without one, to authority. A registered policy never changes; a new version is registered under a new identifier. Readers, identified by their DID, receive access rights through signed access grants that last at most 365 days: legitimateInterest is granted by the economic operator for its own passports, authority only by issuers on the published list of authority issuers. The issuer revokes a grant over the API with immediate effect. In addition, the operator of the service can revoke any grant on order, with a recorded reason, and can withdraw an authority issuer as a whole by removing it from that list.

items.title: Access to controlled data is logged tamper-evidently
items.statement: The service keeps an access log with one entry for every read of the controlled part of a passport by a reader with access rights, every refused read by a reader with a valid token but no valid grant, every read the service makes at the custodian under its own read grant, and every registration and revocation of an access grant. An answer that hands out controlled data is sent only after its entry is written. Entries are only ever added; the service neither changes nor deletes them, the database refuses changes and deletions, and entries are kept for five years. Owners, readers and grant issuers read the entries that concern them through the API; the operator of the service sees the whole log. The log protects against changes made through the service, not against direct changes to its database.

items.title: Actors reading controlled data are identified by a globally unique identifier
items.statement: Every party that authenticates to the service is identified by a W3C Decentralized Identifier: economic operators that write passports, readers of the controlled part and issuers of access grants. Each presents a self-issued JWT (EdDSA) signed with the document key of its own did:oyd, with iss and sub set to that DID, this service as aud, and a lifetime of at most 15 minutes and is accepted once; the service resolves the DID and verifies the signature against the key in its DID document. There are no local accounts, shared logins or shared secrets. A did:oyd is the hash of its own DID document and therefore unique without a central registry. Passport ownership, access grants and every entry of the access log are keyed by this DID, and towards a custodian the service authenticates with its own DID in the same way, with a delegation signed by the economic operator, a client assertion and DPoP. Tokens are verified with DPP_AUTH_MODE=did, as on the hosted instance; a stand-alone instance in the default mode does not verify them. A DID proves control of a key, not the legal identity behind it.

items.title: Custody by a data intermediation service is documented
items.statement: The hosted instance of the service, operated by OwnYourData, keeps no passport documents in its own database: it stores them in a hosting pod of DID Daten-Intermediär-Dienste FlexCo, a separate legal person, and keeps only an index and the storage configuration. For economic operators, the intermediary holds their passports in a collection of its pod and serves the public part to anyone who reads it; a change of custodian moves a passport without changing its product identifier. DID Daten-Intermediär-Dienste FlexCo is notified in Austria as a provider of data intermediation services and listed in the EU register of data intermediation services. The role is described in the documentation of the service: https://github.com/OwnYourData/dpp-service-public/blob/8fec06ed3a108586b254fa4ba7d9a3f174c0f122/README.md#hosted-instance

items.title: Access is limited against attacks and mass scraping
items.statement: The public part of a passport is readable without credentials, as EN 18239:2026 provides; the service limits how fast it can be harvested and keeps the controlled part out of reach. Reads and writes are rate-limited per client address and minute, by default 600 reads and 60 writes, counted in the database all replicas share, and answered above the limit with 429 and Retry-After. No operation lists passports: a read needs a passport identifier, a did:oyd that cannot be guessed, or a product identifier, and the bulk lookup ReadDPPIdsByProductIds takes at most 1000 product identifiers per request and returns identifiers only, at most 1000 per page. The controlled part is handed out only against a verified DID token and a valid access grant, and every such read and every refused read with a valid token is logged; a fine-granular read of an element path beyond the reader's access rights answers 401 without a token and 403 with a valid one, whether or not the element exists. Writes need the owner's signed token, and browsers may write only from configured origins, none by default. The hosted instance serves the API over HTTPS only and refuses HTTP versions below HTTP/2; tokens are bound to this service, live at most 15 minutes and are accepted once, their jti being recorded until they expire, and DID resolution is cached, failures included, so invented DIDs cannot force unbounded lookups. Not covered: the rate limit is kept per client address, so scraping spread over many addresses is not stopped; there is no bot detection; product identifiers that follow a predictable series can be enumerated at the rate limit; and passports held by a custodian are served from the custodian's host under the custodian's protection, not this service's. When the service cannot keep the count for the rate limit, it lets requests through without the limit and logs a warning.
